title: Keeping fitness with less
goal: Plan how to hold endurance fitness through a busy spell, holiday, illness or injury by cutting frequency and volume, keeping intensity, and cross-training.

steps.title: Cut how often and how long
steps.text:
[Reduced training](g:reduced-training) is the alternative to stopping. Classic studies trained young adults for 10 weeks (40 min a day, 6 days a week, cycling and running), then cut one thing for 15 weeks:

- **Frequency** down to 4 or 2 days a week, same intensity and duration: [VO₂max](g:vo2max) stayed at trained levels [[c:red-freq]].
- **Duration** down to 26 or 13 min a day: VO₂max held. Endurance for 2 h or more held at 26 min but fell at 13 min (139 to 123 min, reported as 10%) [[c:red-dur]].

So you can cut a lot of time. But long endurance is the first thing to slip when sessions get short.

claims.text: Training 4 or 2 days a week instead of 6, at the same intensity and duration, kept VO₂max at trained levels for 15 weeks.

evidence.quote: VO2max in the 4 d/wk and 2 d/wk groups remained essentially the same as the trained levels when determined at 5-wk intervals of reduced training.

claims.text: Cutting sessions from 40 to 26 or 13 min kept VO₂max; endurance of 2 h or more held at 26 min but fell 10% at 13 min.

evidence.quote: After reduced training, VO2 max continued to remain at the training levels in both groups.
Long-term endurance (2 h or more) remained the same in the 26-min group but decreased significantly (10%, 139-123 min) in the 13-min group.

steps.title: How much time was cut?
steps.problem: In the frequency study, people trained 40 min a day, 6 days a week, then 40 min, 2 days a week. By what percentage did their weekly training time fall?
steps: Before: 40 × 6 = 240 min a week. After: 40 × 2 = 80 min a week.
As a share of the starting time: 160 ÷ 240 = 0.67, so 67% less time, and VO₂max held.
Divide by the starting value (240), not the new one (80): 160 ÷ 80 = 200% would be wrong.

steps.title: Intensity is the one to keep
steps.text:
The same lab then cut **intensity** by one third or two thirds, keeping frequency and duration. With one third less, VO₂max fell (but stayed above pre-training) and long endurance dropped 21%; with two thirds less, the losses were bigger. The mass of the heart's left [ventricle](g:ventricle), up about 15% with training, went back to baseline in both groups [[c:red-int]].

A review of these maintenance studies sums up: endurance can be kept for up to 15 weeks with as few as 2 sessions a week, or 33–66% less volume (13–26 min a session), *as long as intensity is kept* [[c:red-review]]. Of the three knobs, intensity is the one not to turn down.

claims.text: Cutting training intensity by a third or two thirds failed to keep VO₂max, long endurance and left ventricular mass at trained levels.

evidence.quote: VO2 max was not maintained at the 6-day/wk training levels with a one-third reduction in training intensity but was still higher than pretraining levels.
Long-term endurance was decreased significantly from training by 21% in the one-third reduced group (184-145 min) and by 30% in the two-thirds reduced group (202-141 min).
Calculated left ventricular mass, obtained from echocardiographic measurements, increased approximately 15% after training but returned to control levels after reduced training in both groups.

claims.text: Endurance performance can be kept for up to 15 weeks with 2 sessions a week or 33–66% less volume, as long as intensity is maintained.

evidence.quote: In general populations, endurance performance can be maintained for up to 15 weeks when training frequency is reduced to as little as 2 sessions per week or when exercise volume is reduced by 33-66% (as low as 13-26 minutes per session), as long as exercise intensity (exercising heart rate) is maintained.

steps.title: What about trained athletes?
steps.text:
The review warns there are too few data to make specific advice for athletes [[c:red-gap]]. Two small studies point the same way. Ten well-trained runners cut weekly distance by 70% (81 to 24 km) for 3 weeks, keeping some fast intervals: 5-km race times and VO₂max didn't change [[c:red-houmard]].

Nine endurance athletes went further: one 35-min [HIIT](g:hiit) session a week instead of 6–10 hours, for 4 weeks. VO₂max didn't change, but [time to exhaustion](g:time-to-exhaustion) at 75% of VO₂max fell 21%, from 79 to 62 min [[c:red-madsen]].

VO₂max is the sturdy part. Long endurance needs more volume to hold, so a VO₂max test can miss what you've lost.

claims.text: There are too few data for specific maintenance advice for athletes.

evidence.quote: Insufficient data exists to make specific recommendations for athletes or military personnel.

claims.text: Well-trained runners who cut volume by 70% for 3 weeks while keeping intervals kept their 5-km times and VO₂max.

evidence.quote: The runners then reduced weekly training volume (RT) by 70% of BT to 24 +/- 2 km/week and frequency by 17% to 5 days/week for 3 weeks.

No significant (P greater than 0.05) changes occurred with RT in body weight, % body fat, overall 5 km race times, VO2max, muscular power (vertical leap and Margaria power test), and citrate synthase activity (at 2 weeks of RT).

claims.text: One 35-min high-intensity session a week for 4 weeks kept VO₂max but cut time to exhaustion at 75% VO₂max by 21%.

evidence.quote: Detraining had no effect on VO2max (4.57 +/- 0.10 vs. 4.54 +/- 0.08 l/min), but endurance capacity decreased by 21% from 79 +/- 4 to 62 +/- 4 min (P < 0.001).

steps.title: Injured? Cross-train
steps.text:
When you can't do your sport, do another: [cross-training](g:cross-training). In trained runners, 6 weeks of [deep-water running](g:deep-water-running), with the same hard and long sessions as on land, kept VO₂max and [running economy](g:running-economy) as well as treadmill running did [[c:red-dwr]]. In another trial, trained people who switched from running to water running or cycling for 6 weeks kept their 2-mile race time as well as those who kept running [[c:red-eyestone]].

The review's advice: athletes should cross-train in a mode close to their sport, while less-trained people can also gain from very different ones. With one limb in a cast, training the other may also limit the loss in the immobilised one [[c:red-cross-review]].

claims.text: Six weeks of deep-water running kept aerobic performance (VO₂max, running economy) in trained runners as well as land running.

evidence.quote: It was concluded that deep water running may serve as an effective training alternative to landbased running for the maintenance of aerobic performance for up to 6 wk in trained endurance athletes.

claims.text: Over 6 weeks, water running or cycling kept 2-mile run performance as well as running did.

evidence.quote: It was concluded that over a 6-week period, runners who cannot run because of soft tissue injury can maintain VO2max and 2-mile run performance similar to running training with either cycling or water running.

claims.text: Athletes should cross-train in a similar mode; moderately trained people can also benefit from dissimilar modes; training the opposite limb may limit detraining during one-limb immobilisation.

evidence.quote: Athletes should use similar-mode exercise, but moderately trained individuals could also benefit from dissimilar-mode cross-training.
Finally, the existence of a cross-transfer effect between ipsilateral and contralateral limbs should be considered in order to limit detraining during periods of unilateral immobilisation.

points: To keep fitness through a busy spell, cut frequency (down to 2 sessions a week) or duration (by a third to two thirds), not intensity.
Cutting intensity by a third already lost VO₂max, long endurance and heart growth.
VO₂max is the sturdy part; endurance for 2 h or more slips first when sessions get short or rare.
Data in trained athletes are few: runners cutting volume 70% for 3 weeks kept race times, while one HIIT session a week kept VO₂max but not long endurance.
Injured? Cross-train in a mode close to your sport: deep-water running or cycling kept runners' fitness for 6 weeks.

variants.stem: A cyclist usually trains 5 × 60 min a week. In a busy month she trains 2 × 60 min. By what percentage has she cut her weekly time?

options.why: 40% is the share she still trains, not the share she cut.
This divides the cut (180) by the new time (120) instead of the starting time.
67% is the cut in the frequency study (6 to 2 days), not hers.

variants.stem: A runner usually trains 6 × 50 min a week. During exams he trains 4 × 45 min. By what percentage has he cut his weekly time?

options.why: 60% is the share he still trains, not the share he cut.
This adds the separate cuts (33% fewer days + 10% shorter sessions); cuts multiply, they don't add.
This divides the cut (120) by the new time (180) instead of the starting time.

variants.stem: A triathlete usually trains 8 h a week. On a work trip she manages 3 h. By what percentage has she cut her weekly time?

options.why: 38% is the share she still trains, not the share she cut.
This divides the cut (5 h) by the new time (3 h) instead of the starting time.
5 is the cut in hours, not a percentage.

variants.stem: A marathoner can only run 15 min a day for 3 months instead of 45, at the same pace and days. What does the duration study predict?

options.text: VO₂max may hold, but 2-hour endurance will likely fall
options.why: Right: at 13 min a day VO₂max held, but endurance of 2 h or more fell (139 to 123 min).

options.text: Everything holds, as long as the pace is kept
options.why: Short-term endurance and VO₂max held, but long endurance did not at the shortest duration.

options.text: VO₂max falls first, long endurance holds
options.why: It's the other way round: VO₂max was the measure that held.

options.text: All gains are lost, as with a full stop
options.why: Short daily sessions kept VO₂max at trained levels for 15 weeks.

variants.stem: A cyclist has 6 busy weeks at work and can train at most 3 h a week instead of 8. Which plan best protects his fitness?

options.text: Three shorter sessions, keeping his usual intervals
options.why: Right: frequency and volume can drop a lot if intensity is kept.

options.text: Three hours of easy riding, saving intervals for later
options.why: Cutting intensity is what lost VO₂max and endurance in the maintenance studies.

options.text: One easy 3-h ride each Sunday
options.why: This drops intensity, the one cut that lost fitness, and goes below the 2 sessions a week that held VO₂max.

options.text: Stop fully and catch up after
options.why: Six weeks off means long-term detraining, which costs far more than reduced training.

variants.stem: In the intensity study, what happened to the left ventricle's mass when training intensity was cut?

options.text: It went back to pre-training levels
options.why: Right: it rose about 15% with training and returned to control levels in both reduced groups.

options.text: It stayed enlarged, since frequency held
options.why: Frequency and duration were kept, but the heart's growth was still lost.

options.text: It kept growing with the long sessions
options.why: Sessions stayed 40 min; there were no longer sessions.

options.text: It fell below pre-training levels
options.why: It returned to control levels, not below them.

variants.stem: A triathlete has a 2-week holiday with only a hotel gym bike. Based on these studies, which plan makes most sense?

options.text: Two or three short, hard sessions a week
options.why: Right: much less volume is fine for a few weeks if some intensity is kept.

options.text: Nothing: 2 weeks off costs nothing
options.why: Even 2–4 weeks off cost trained men about 6% of VO₂max, mostly through lost plasma volume.

options.text: An easy hour a day, no intensity at all
options.why: Dropping intensity is the cut that loses fitness.

options.text: Three hours a day to bank fitness
options.why: Large extra volume on holiday isn't needed to hold fitness for 2 weeks.

variants.stem: With one HIIT session a week for 4 weeks, athletes kept their VO₂max but lost 21% of their time to exhaustion at 75% VO₂max. What does this show?

options.text: Long endurance can fall while VO₂max holds
options.why: Right: VO₂max is the sturdy part; a VO₂max test alone would have missed the loss.

options.text: The VO₂max test must have been faulty
options.why: VO₂max often holds on little training; the result fits the duration studies too.

options.text: HIIT harms endurance
options.why: HIIT was the only training kept; the loss came from dropping 6–10 h of volume.

options.text: Endurance time doesn't depend on training
options.why: It fell by 21% when training was cut, so it clearly does.

variants.stem: The "keep intensity" rule rests mostly on the three Hickson studies. What most limits applying them to a trained cyclist?

options.text: About 12 young adults per study, trained only 10 weeks
options.why: Right: small groups of recently trained people; the review says data in athletes are too few.

options.text: They tested VO₂max only on a bike
options.why: VO₂max was measured both cycling and on a treadmill.

options.text: They lasted only a week
options.why: Each reduced-training period lasted 15 weeks.

options.text: They didn't include strength training
options.why: Strength wasn't the question; the limit is who was studied.

variants.stem: A runner has a shin stress fracture and can't run for 6 weeks; her doctor allows non-impact exercise. Which plan best keeps her running fitness?

options.text: Deep-water running with her usual hard and long sessions
options.why: Right: 6 weeks of pool running with the same session mix kept trained runners' VO₂max and economy.

options.text: Easy swimming a few times a week
options.why: A very different mode at low intensity: the review advises a similar mode for athletes, with intensity kept.

options.text: No exercise at all until she can run
options.why: Six weeks off is long-term detraining; non-impact training avoids most of that loss.

options.text: Upper-body weights only
options.why: This keeps little of her running-specific aerobic fitness.

variants.stem: According to the review, who can also gain from cross-training in a very different mode, such as rowing for a runner?

options.text: Moderately trained people
options.why: Right: athletes should stick to a similar mode, while moderately trained people can also benefit from dissimilar ones.

options.text: Elite runners
options.why: The review advises athletes to use a mode similar to their sport.

options.text: Nobody: cross-training never helps
options.why: Water running and cycling both kept runners' fitness for 6 weeks.

options.text: Only people with one limb in a cast
options.why: Training the other limb is a separate point (cross-transfer), not about very different sports.
